procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated in the provided text, but it can be inferred that the case originated with an FIR (First Information Report) which led to criminal applications.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated 10.07.2017 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court, partly allowing the criminal applications.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court partly allowed the criminal applications. It quashed the FIR in relation to some offences alleged against the accused but declined to quash the entire FIR. The High Court's observations in an earlier round of litigation were also considered.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Both the complainants and the accused persons felt aggrieved by the High Court's judgment and filed appeals in the Supreme Court by way of special leave. The complainants appealed because their appeals were dismissed, and the accused appealed because the High Court did not quash the entire FIR.

directions: The appeals filed by the complainants, i.e., criminal appeals @ S.L.P. (Crl.) Nos. 5476 & 5475 of 2017 are allowed.
The impugned judgment is set aside.
The appeals filed by the accused persons, i.e., criminal appeals @ S.L.P.(Crl.) Nos. 5155, 5322, 5500 & 5867/2017 are dismissed.
As a consequence, the criminal applications filed by the accused persons under Section 482 of the Code out of which these appeals arise are dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, while exercising its inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., can act like an investigating or appellate authority to quash an FIR.

facts: The High Court, exercising its powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., was asked to quash an FIR.

Instead of quashing it entirely or upholding it, the High Court quashed the FIR in part for certain offenses (u/ss.406, 420, 120B IPC and the SC/ST Act) but allowed the investigation to continue for other alleged offenses (bogus powers of attorney, blackmail, etc.).
In reaching this decision, the High Court went into the "minutest details" of the case, resulting in an 89-page judgment.
law: The jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is limited to examining whether the factual contents of an FIR disclose a 'prima facie' commission of a cognizable offense.
If a prima facie case is disclosed, the High Court must "stay its hand" and allow the investigating agency to conduct its probe.
The High Court's inherent powers under Section 482 cannot be equated with the powers of an investigating agency or an appellate court.
These inherent powers cannot be stretched to any extent and must be exercised within the parameters laid down by the Supreme Court.
application: The Supreme Court found that the FIR, when read as a whole, did disclose a prima facie commission of various cognizable offenses.

By dissecting the FIR, deciding which parts were good and which were bad, and quashing it in part, the High Court acted like an investigating or appellate authority, which is beyond its jurisdiction under Section 482.
The High Court wrongly decided substantive issues of the case at the initial stage, instead of limiting its review to a prima facie assessment.
The very fact that the High Court delved into minute details and wrote an 89-page judgment to partially quash the FIR was seen as clear evidence that it had exceeded its limited jurisdiction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court exceeded its inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. It held that a High Court cannot act like an investigating or appellate authority to minutely examine and quash an FIR in part. Once it is found that the FIR discloses a prima facie cognizable offense, the High Court should not interfere and must allow the investigation to proceed on the entire FIR.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, while exercising its inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., can act like an investigating or appellate authority to quash an FIR.
appellant_arguments: The counsel for the complainants argued that there was no legal justification for the High Court to have quashed the FIR in part, and that part of the judgment should be set aside.
respondent_arguments: The counsel for the accused persons argued that the entire FIR is an abuse of the legal process and does not make out a prima facie case.
They contended that the matter had already been settled in writing and the complainants had accepted a huge consideration, leaving no cause for a belated FIR.
They relied on several documents and observations from a prior round of litigation to show that the FIR should be quashed.
They cited two Supreme Court decisions, (2015) 11 SCC 730 and (2011) 3 SCC 351, to support their contentions.

cases.case_name: State of West Bengal & Ors. vs. Swapan Kumar Guha & Ors.
cases.principle: The inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 cannot be stretched to any extent and cannot be equated with the appellate powers of the High Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inherent powers of the High Court cannot be stretched to any extent and cannot be equated with the appellate powers of the High Court; the parameters laid down for exercising inherent powers must be kept in mind to avoid committing a jurisdictional error.
obiter: This order should not be construed as having decided any issue on merits, and investigating authorities should not be influenced by any observations made by the lower courts or the High Court in their respective orders while investigating the matter.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On perusal of the three complaints and the FIR mentioned above, we are of the considered view that the complaint and FIR, do disclose a prima facie commission of various cognizable offences alleged by the complainants against the accused persons and, therefore, the High Court instead of dismissing the application filed by the accused persons in part should have dismissed the application as a whole to uphold the entire FIR in question.
legal_tests_applied: Once the Court finds that the FIR does disclose prima facie commission of any cognizable offence, it should stay its hand and allow the investigating machinery to step in to initiate the investigation to stop the investigation, for to do so would be to trench upon the lawful power of the police to investigate into cognizable offences.
why_appellant_lost: The Supreme Court found that the two decisions relied upon by the accused persons were distinguishable on facts, as they involved complaints filed in court under specific acts, not an FIR, and the decisions turned on the specific facts of those cases.

The court rejected the accused's contention that the FIR did not make out a prima facie case, stating, "we are of the considered view that the complaint and FIR, do disclose a prima facie commission of various cognizable offences alleged by the complainants against the accused persons."
why_respondent_won: The Supreme Court accepted the complainants' submission that there was no legal justification for the High Court to have quashed the FIR in part, finding that the High Court should have dismissed the accused's application as a whole.

The court found that since the FIR disclosed a prima facie commission of cognizable offenses, the High Court should have followed the established legal principle to "stay its hand and allow the investigating machinery to step in" rather than quashing parts of it.
policy_considerations: The court should not trench upon the lawful power of the police to investigate into cognizable offences once a prima facie case is disclosed in the FIR.

The court, while deciding on quashing an FIR, should refrain from making observations on the merits or giving reasoning on factual issues, as it may cause prejudice to the parties and hamper the on-going investigation process.

It is improper for a High Court, while exercising its jurisdiction under Section 482, to conduct a detailed, lengthy examination of the facts to determine which parts of an FIR are valid, as this is the role of the investigating agency.
